narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted, signaling consistently weak academic performance in law school. 

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure. A score of 23.5 is substantially lower than the average of 37 among accepted applicants, indicating the model saw this as a clear risk for bar exam success.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential feature, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 2.3 it is well below the accepted average of 3.23, yet the model treated this relatively low GPA as slightly encouraging compared with the rest of your profile.

Taken together, your low class rankings and LSAT score outweighed the modest positive signal from your GPA, leading to the rejection.

What you should do next is focus on improving your academic record and retaking the LSAT. Raising both your class performance and test score would directly address the factors that most hurt your prediction and give you a much stronger chance on a future application.
